name: Declan Whitmore
presenting_complaint: Fever, severe headache and neck stiffness, now drowsy with a rash

medical_history.social: University student living in shared college accommodation. Non-smoker, social alcohol. No recent travel.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 24-year-old male university student is brought to ED by housemates with a 12-hour history of fever, severe frontal headache, neck stiffness and photophobia, now increasingly drowsy. Obs: BP 84/48, HR 128, RR 26, SpO2 93% on air, temp 39.6, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). A spreading non-blanching purpuric rash is noted on the trunk and legs. He is a well, previously fit man in shared college accommodation.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Onset and 12-hour progression of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia
Altered conscious state / drowsiness reported by housemates (collateral history)
Non-blanching rash noticed and progressing — screen for meningococcaemia
Red-flag screen: seizures, focal neurology, vomiting, recent head injury
Risk factors: shared college accommodation / close-contact living, vaccination status (meningococcal ACWY/B), immunocompromise, recent travel
Allergy history (specifically penicillin/cephalosporin) before empirical antibiotics
Key negatives: not immunosuppressed, not pregnant, no anticoagulation
objective: A-to-E assessment; document GCS with breakdown (E3 V4 M6 = 13) and pupils
Full set of vitals documenting sepsis: hypotension 84/48, tachycardia 128, tachypnoea 26, fever 39.6, SpO2 93%
Meningism signs: neck stiffness, Kernig/Brudzinski, photophobia
Skin exam for non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (tumbler/glass test), map spread
Bedside glucose (BGL 6.4) and venous/arterial blood gas with lactate
Blood cultures drawn (before or alongside first antibiotic dose if no delay), plus FBC, UEC, CRP, coags, meningococcal/pneumococcal PCR
assessment: Bacterial meningitis with sepsis / septic shock — likely meningococcal (meningococcaemia given purpuric rash)
Differential: pneumococcal meningitis, other bacterial meningitis; consider viral (HSV) encephalitis
Other DDx to document/exclude: subarachnoid haemorrhage, cerebral abscess
Septic shock with hypotension refractory to consideration for fluid resuscitation
plan: GIVE EMPIRICAL ANTIBIOTICS IMMEDIATELY — do NOT delay for CT or LP: ceftriaxone 2 g IV stat (child dosing 100 mg/kg if applicable)
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or just before the first antibiotic dose

Add vancomycin (e.g. 25-30 mg/kg IV loading) per local guideline for possible resistant pneumococcus; add benzylpenicillin/amoxicillin for Listeria cover if >50, immunosuppressed or pregnant (not required here but document the reasoning)
Activate sepsis pathway: IV access x2, blood cultures, lactate, IV crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL-1 L, reassess), target MAP >=65 and escalate to vasopressors if fluid-refractory
Droplet precautions and isolate the patient
CT brain BEFORE LP given reduced GCS (GCS 13) — but antibiotics are given first regardless; defer LP until safe/stable
Escalate early: notify ED consultant, ICU and Infectious Diseases
Notify public health — meningococcal disease is a notifiable condition; arrange contact prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin/rifampicin) for close contacts and document

critical_errors: Delaying empirical antibiotics (ceftriaxone) to wait for CT brain or lumbar puncture in suspected bacterial meningitis with sepsis — antibiotics (and dexamethasone) must be given immediately; this loses the case
must_not_miss: Sepsis / septic shock recognition and escalation (sepsis pathway, fluids, ICU referral)
Meningococcaemia — recognise the non-blanching purpuric rash and treat as meningococcal disease
Dexamethasone given with or before the first antibiotic dose
Notifiable-disease action: public health notification, droplet precautions and contact prophylaxis documented
